newsitem.title: UK: Seeking votes at home, UK's Major bars outsiders.
newsitem.headline: Seeking votes at home, UK's Major bars outsiders.

text.p: Britain lived up to its "little Englander" reputation on Wednesday when the ruling Conservatives banned Europeans from the launch of their election manifesto.
The French fumed. The Dutch opted to grin and bear it while weary German journalists blamed age-old British xenophobia.

"This reinforces all the prejudices about Britain's isolationism. Obviously the Conservatives' defence against the rest of Europe starts here and now at Conservative Central Office," said Tina van Houts, a Dutch journalist.

The fracas began when the Conservative Party summoned journalists to the unveiling of its manifesto: the core ideas on which it will fight the May 1 election, not least among them plans for European economic integration and NATO enlargement.
Prime Minister John Major spoke of "a confident, united and sovereign nation" and of a Britain that was "the best place in the world to live".
Indeed, no sooner had the doors closed behind him, that a furious foreign press corps questioned Britain's fabled sense of fair play and Major's pledge to stay at the heart of Europe.
"For us on the continent, this is the most important European election this year and we should have been allowed access," said Theo Zoll, bureau chief of German television ZDF.
The angry outcasts said it was typical of a party riven by infighting over European integration and a country that enjoys a love-hate relationship with many of its closest neighbours.
They even lodged a formal complaint with Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, saying such shenanigans never happen back home.

"We have no prejudices like the stereotypes say," said Reinhart Haecker of Germany's Stuttgarter Zeitung. "It never happens in our country that a British person is excluded and we expect to be handled the same way in this country, especially after Mr Major told us he will be at the heart of Europe."
"I'm disgusted but not surprised," said Etienne Duval, who works for French, German, Belgian and Swiss television.
"They say there are no votes in France and when MPs talk to us, they more often than not ask for 50 pounds ($82) or more. It's only money that gets most of them to talk to us in Europe."
The Conservatives, already caught up in cash-for-questions scandals on a much grander scale, said the dispute was over space, and nothing seamier.

"This room only seats 300," said one top aide to Major. "While we don't want to be too ruthless and I know we have upset some of your friends, this manifesto is, after all, addressed to the people in the British elections -- to our voters."

As for what the perceived snub said about Britain's often testy relations with Europe -- the continentals were especially incensed to see U.S. journalists win entry -- the Major aide bristled at talk of favouritism or xenophobia.
"Complete and utter rubbish. There was no vetting. It was a case of numbers and nothing else," said the aide.
